183.title: No hiding place (123–128)
183.hook: poison can't harm a hand without a wound; not in the sky, the sea or a mountain cave is there escape from one's deeds
183.howItsDone: Buddhists understand kamma as the natural result of intentional action rather than a punishment handed down, and many practice confessing faults and taking the precepts again as a way of closing the wound rather than hiding it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the water-pot that fills drop by drop, with harm or with good. Your line: drop by drop.

Everybody has a drawer. Maybe a real one, stuffed with the letter you never answered. Maybe a folder on your phone, or a conversation you've steered around for years. And there's a hope that goes with it: if I move far enough away, change jobs, start fresh somewhere nobody knows me, it won't follow. Sometimes a new start really helps. But there's one thing a moving truck can't leave behind, and the Dhammapada names it with three places people run to: the sky, the sea and a mountain cave.
screen: `EVERYBODY HAS A DRAWER.` → `A FRESH START SOMEWHERE ELSE.` → `THE SKY, THE SEA, A CAVE.`

segments.voice: Chapter nine ends with pictures of protection. Verse one twenty-three: a merchant carrying much wealth with few companions avoids a dangerous road, the way someone who loves life avoids poison. Then a strange, lovely image, verse one twenty-four: "He who has no wound on his hand, may touch poison with his hand; poison does not affect one who has no wound; nor is there evil for one who does not commit evil." The harm gets in through the wound. Close the wound, and the poison has nowhere to enter. Verse one twenty-five adds that harm aimed at an innocent person blows back on the one who threw it, "like light dust thrown up against the wind." Then the heart of today, verse one twenty-seven: "Not in the sky, not in the midst of the sea, not if we enter into the clefts of the mountains, is there known a spot in the whole world where a man might be freed from an evil deed." Nobody is hunting you down. In Buddhist teaching, kamma isn't a judge sending out a posse. The deed comes along because you're the one who did it; it goes wherever you go. That can sound grim, but good deeds travel with you just as surely. Verse one twenty-eight uses the same three places for death: no spot in the world escapes it. So the chapter doesn't point toward a better hiding place. It points back to the hand and the wound: fewer wounds, less poison, less to hide.

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open in your lap and look at them; no need to find a wound. Close your eyes and ask, gently: is there something I'd rather hide? You don't have to open the whole drawer: notice that it's there, and how the body feels, with no scolding, because seeing it is the first step toward closing the wound. Then come back to the breath, with nothing to run from.

Your line: fewer wounds, less poison. The way out isn't a place. That's day one hundred eighty-three.

184.title: All tremble (129–132)
184.hook: all tremble at the rod, all fear death; putting yourself in their place, do not kill
184.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers cite these verses as a basis of the first precept, refraining from taking life, which covers animals as well as people; some practitioners carry insects outside rather than kill them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, papa: not the sky, not the sea, not a mountain cave frees you from a deed. Your line: fewer wounds, less poison. Today, chapter ten begins.

Raise your hand quickly near a dog that's been hit before, and it flinches. Slam a door in a house with a toddler, and the whole small body jumps. A pigeon on the sidewalk scatters when your foot comes down too near. Nobody taught them that. The flinch comes before any thought. Chapter ten of the Dhammapada is called punishment, and it starts right there, with the flinch that everyone shares.
screen: `THE DOG THAT FLINCHES.` → `THE TODDLER AT THE SLAMMED DOOR.` → `THE FLINCH EVERYONE SHARES.`

segments.voice: Its Pali name is Daṇḍavagga. A daṇḍa is a stick, a rod, a staff: the thing you're hit with, and so, punishment. Verse one twenty-nine, in Max Müller's words: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter." Müller wrote all men, but the Pali word is simply sabbe, all, and some readers hear it as all beings: the dog, the pigeon, the fish on the hook. At the heart of the verse is a short Pali phrase meaning, roughly, making yourself the comparison. Fear is known from the inside, so your own fear says what it's like for them. No complicated philosophy. Just your own flinch, turned outward. This is the root of the first precept, the training to refrain from taking life, from camp three. Verse one thirty gives it a gentler turn: "all men love life." Verses one thirty-one and one thirty-two make the same point about happiness. Everyone, the text says, longs for it. One who seeks their own happiness by harming beings who also long for happiness, Müller writes, "will not find happiness after death." One who doesn't harm them will. That's the chapter's method, and it's imagination: before you raise the rod, feel yourself on the other end of it.

segments.voice: Remember a moment when you were afraid, not the worst one, a small one: a near miss in traffic, a raised voice, a letter you dreaded opening, and feel where the fear lived in your body. Now bring to mind someone else, a person or an animal, who might feel that same flinch today, maybe because of you, maybe not. For a few breaths, put yourself in their place, let your fear and theirs be the same fear, then rest in the breath.
All tremble. Verse one twenty-nine: all tremble at the rod, all fear death, so, making yourself the comparison, do not kill.
Your line: all fear the rod. The flinch is shared. One hundred eighty-four days now.

185.title: The broken gong (133–136)
185.hook: speak no harsh words; be silent as a broken gong and you have reached peace
185.howItsDone: Right speech, one of the steps of the eightfold path, includes refraining from harsh words, and Buddhist teachers often use the broken gong as an image for letting provocation land without answering in kind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, all tremble: every creature flinches at the rod. Your line: all fear the rod.

Somebody in the group chat says something sharp. Thumbs start moving before the mind has caught up. The reply gets typed, and it's good. Clever. It lands. Then a reply to the reply, someone else joins in, and forty messages later nobody remembers what the first one said. Every sharp word got an answer, and every answer got an answer. It's like hitting a bell: strike it, and it rings back at you. Today's verse offers a different kind of bell, one that doesn't ring back at all.
screen: `THE SHARP MESSAGE.` → `FORTY REPLIES LATER.` → `A BELL THAT RINGS BACK.`

segments.voice: Verse one thirty-three could have been written about that group chat. In Max Müller's words: "Do not speak harshly to anybody; those who are spoken to will answer thee in the same way. Angry speech is painful, blows for blows will touch thee." Harsh words come back. That's not a threat; it's an observation anyone can check. Then the image. Verse one thirty-four: "If, like a shattered metal plate (gong), thou utter not, then thou hast reached Nirvana; contention is not known to thee." Müller added the word gong in brackets. The Pali word, kaṃsa, names bronze, a bronze vessel or plate, the kind that rings when struck. A whole gong answers every blow. A cracked one doesn't: a dull thud, then nothing. No echo, no second round. This isn't the silence of sulking, which rings for days on the inside. It isn't swallowing everything forever. It's the quiet of something that no longer needs to answer back, and the verse is bold about it: such quiet is already nirvana, and quarrel doesn't know where to find you. Then the chapter turns sober. Verse one thirty-five: "As a cowherd with his staff drives his cows into the stable, so do Age and Death drive the life of men." Life is short, and the cowherd is already walking. One more reason not to spend it on the fortieth reply.

segments.voice: Remember a recent moment when someone's words stung and you answered back, and replay only the first line, theirs. This time, picture yourself as the cracked gong: the words arrive and land, and nothing rings, while you watch the urge to answer rise in your chest or jaw like a wave coming in and going out. You don't have to agree with them; you just don't ring.
Kamsa. Bronze: the broken gong of verse one thirty-four, cracked so it no longer rings, like one who doesn't answer back and so finds peace.
Your line: silent as a broken gong. No echo, and no second round. Until tomorrow.

186.title: Fashion yourself (137–145)
186.hook: irrigators lead water, fletchers bend arrows, carpenters bend wood; the good fashion themselves
186.howItsDone: Buddhist training is often described as gradual, like a craftsman's work: keeping precepts, sitting daily and guarding the senses, rather than dramatic acts of self-denial, which the Buddha is remembered as having tried and set aside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kamsa, the broken gong: a cracked bronze plate that doesn't ring back. Your line: silent as a broken gong.

A potter centers clay on the wheel. A gardener trains a vine along a fence, a little each week. A woodworker steams a strip of oak until it will bend into the curve of a chair. None of them fight the material. None of them finish in a day. They lead it, patiently, toward a shape. The last verse of chapter ten gathers three craftsmen like that, and then adds a fourth, whose material is the self.
screen: `A POTTER, A GARDENER, A WOODWORKER.` → `THEY LEAD THE MATERIAL.` → `A FOURTH CRAFTSMAN.`

segments.voice: First, chapter ten names what doesn't work. Verse one forty-one lists the dramatic ascetic practices of the Buddha's day and says none of them purify anyone on their own: "Not nakedness, not platted hair, not dirt, not fasting, or lying on the earth, not rubbing with dust, not sitting motionless, can purify a mortal who has not overcome desires." The traditional story of his life says the Buddha had tried severe austerities himself before his awakening, and set them aside. Show doesn't shape the mind. Then comes a well-trained horse that needs only a touch of the whip to get moving, and the text asks: is anyone that responsive to correction? Then the craftsmen. Verse one forty-five: "Well-makers lead the water (wherever they like); fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; good people fashion themselves." Müller says well-makers; the Pali word is often translated irrigators, the people who dig channels and lead water across fields. A fletcher is an arrow-maker, who heats and straightens a shaft until it flies true. Almost the same verse appeared back in chapter six, verse eighty, about the wise. The Pali verb at the end means to tame or train, the way you'd train a young horse. Together, the images make a quiet, practical picture of change. Water isn't forced uphill; it's given a channel. Wood isn't snapped; it's bent with heat and time. Habits aren't smashed either. You dig a small channel, and dig it again tomorrow.

segments.voice: Choose one habit you'd like to shape, not overhaul: scrolling before bed, interrupting, skipping lunch. Instead of fighting it, picture a small channel beside it, one easy thing that could carry the energy somewhere better, like a book by the pillow, one breath before speaking, or a piece of fruit in your bag. Then let the picture go, and sit with the breath, bending gently toward stillness.
Fashion yourself. Verse one forty-five: irrigators lead water, fletchers bend arrows, carpenters bend wood, and good people shape themselves.
Your line: water led in channels. Not forced, just led, patiently. Day one hundred eighty-six.

187.title: The world is burning (146–150)
187.hook: why laughter, why joy, when the world is always burning; this body a city built of bones
187.howItsDone: Some Buddhist monastics practice reflection on the body and on aging as a way to loosen attachment and vanity, and some lay Buddhists recite a short reflection that aging, sickness and death are natural to everyone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fashion yourself: irrigators, fletchers, carpenters, and good people shaping themselves. Your line: water led in channels. Today, chapter eleven begins: old age.

Look at a photo of yourself from ten years ago. Maybe you laugh at the haircut. Maybe you feel a small pang. The face is you and not quite you. Something has been quietly happening the whole time, day and night, and it hasn't paused once. Chapter eleven of the Dhammapada is called old age, and its first line sounds almost rude, like someone walking into a party and asking why everyone's laughing. It isn't meant as gloom. It's meant as a wake-up.
screen: `A PHOTO FROM TEN YEARS AGO.` → `IT HASN'T PAUSED ONCE.` → `WHY IS EVERYONE LAUGHING?`

segments.voice: Verse one forty-six, in Max Müller's translation: "How is there laughter, how is there joy, as this world is always burning? Why do you not seek a light, ye who are surrounded by darkness?" The Buddha uses burning elsewhere too. In a discourse known as the fire sermon, he tells a thousand monks, once fire-worshippers, that everything is burning: the eye, the ear, the mind, all burning with the fires of greed, hatred and delusion, and with birth, aging and death. If the house is on fire, why keep partying in it? And the verse doesn't say despair. It says: seek a light. The next verses look straight at the body. The old commentary sets verse one forty-seven beside a story. Sirimā, a famous and beautiful courtesan in the city of Rajagaha, died suddenly. The Buddha asked the king to leave her body in the charnel ground for some days and then offer it for sale. At first for a thousand coins. Then for less. Then for nothing. No one would take it. Verse one fifty calls the body a city: "After a stronghold has been made of the bones, it is covered with flesh and blood, and there dwell in it old age and death, pride and deceit." A fortress built of bones, with some uninvited tenants. This is meant to loosen vanity, not to make anyone hate their body. The same tradition calls a human life rare and precious. The point is to see clearly, and then use the time.
screen: `WHY LAUGHTER, IF THE WORLD BURNS?` · `THE FIRE SERMON: ALL IS BURNING.` · `SIRIMĀ: NO ONE WOULD TAKE IT.` · `A CITY BUILT OF BONES.` · then, large: `SEEK A LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and look at them: the lines, the knuckles, maybe a scar you remember getting. These hands have carried groceries, held other hands, typed a thousand messages, and they're changing too, a little every day; look at them kindly, the way you'd look at an old friend's face. Then close your eyes and feel them from the inside, the warmth, the tingling, the pulse: borrowed, not owned, and still good company.
Jara. Old age, decay: verse one forty-six asks why laughter, why joy, when the world is always burning, and says seek a light.
Your line: the world is on fire. The verse's answer is a light. That's one hundred eighty-seven days.

188.title: The house-builder, again (151–156)
188.hook: even royal chariots wear out; one who learns little grows old like an ox; the house-builder verses return
188.howItsDone: The house-builder verses are among the most chanted and memorized in Theravada Buddhism, and are remembered as the Buddha's first words after his awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jara: the world is burning, why laughter, why joy, and a city built of bones. Your line was the world is on fire.

A royal carriage sits in a museum. Gold leaf, velvet seats, carved wheels. Once it carried a king through cheering crowds. Now the gold is flaking, the velvet is thin, and a sign says please do not touch. Even the finest things wear out. Chapter eleven closes with that image, and then does something you might not expect: it brings back a poem you already know, one you first heard more than a hundred and thirty days ago, on the morning of the Buddha's awakening.
screen: `A ROYAL CARRIAGE IN A MUSEUM.` → `EVEN THE FINEST THINGS WEAR OUT.` → `A POEM YOU ALREADY KNOW.`

segments.voice: Verse one fifty-one, in Max Müller's words: "The brilliant chariots of kings are destroyed, the body also approaches destruction, but the virtue of good people never approaches destruction." Things wear out. Goodness doesn't, at least not in the same way. Then a line that's almost funny: "A man who has learnt little, grows old like an ox; his flesh grows, but his knowledge does not grow." Getting older isn't the same as growing. And then, right in the chapter on old age, the house-builder verses, one fifty-three and one fifty-four. Tradition holds they were the Buddha's first words after waking. On day fifty-six we heard them as a victory song at dawn. Read in order, here, they sound different: they're the answer to everything the chapter has said about wearing out. Life after life, a house gets built. Craving is the builder. And then: "maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again. All thy rafters are broken, thy ridge-pole is sundered." The ridgepole is the top beam that holds the whole roof, and the commentaries read it as ignorance. Remove that, and nothing more gets built. The chapter ends with two sad pictures of wasted time: people who never gained the real treasure while young, left like old herons at a lake with no fish, or like broken bows, sighing after the past. The whole chapter says one thing: the house keeps falling down, so find the builder while there's time.

189.title: First yourself (157–160)
189.hook: set yourself in what is right first, then teach others; self is the lord of self
189.howItsDone: In Buddhist communities a teacher's own conduct is expected to match the teaching, and verse 160, attā hi attano nātho, is often quoted to mean that each person is responsible for their own practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the house-builder, again: chariots wear out, and the builder, once seen, builds no more. Your line was the ridgepole is broken. Today closes the week.

You've met this person. The friend who gives brilliant relationship advice and hasn't had a calm week in years. The coach who yells about staying calm. Maybe you've been this person, telling someone to get more sleep at one in the morning. Advice is cheap, and people can usually hear the difference between words that have been lived and words that haven't. Chapter twelve of the Dhammapada is called self, and it opens with a simple order of operations.
screen: `THE FRIEND WITH BRILLIANT ADVICE.` → `GET MORE SLEEP, AT 1 A.M.` → `AN ORDER OF OPERATIONS.`

segments.voice: Verse one fifty-eight, in Max Müller's translation: "Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others; thus a wise man will not suffer." The old commentary pins this verse to a monk named Upananda, who gave eloquent talks about wanting little while quietly collecting robes for himself. The next verse puts it plainly: "If a man make himself as he teaches others to be, then, being himself well subdued, he may subdue (others); one's own self is indeed difficult to subdue." Difficult. The verse doesn't pretend otherwise. Then verse one sixty: "Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord?" In Pali it's short and rhythmic: attā hi attano nātho. A nātha is a protector, a refuge, someone you can lean on. But doesn't Buddhism teach anattā, not-self? Here attā is the ordinary word for oneself, the way English says do it yourself. It's not a claim about a permanent soul. It's a claim about responsibility: no one else can train your mind for you. That fits the whole week. No hiding place from your own deeds, papa. All tremble, so imagine yourself in their place. The broken gong that doesn't answer back, kamsa. Fashion yourself, like water led in channels. The world burning, and the house-builder seen. And today: first yourself.
screen: `FIRST WHAT IS PROPER, THEN TEACH.` · `ONE'S OWN SELF IS HARD TO SUBDUE.` · `ATTĀ HI ATTANO NĀTHO.` · `A WEEK OF DOING IT YOURSELF.` · then, large: `SELF IS LORD OF SELF.`

segments.voice: Think of one piece of advice you often give other people: be patient, put the phone down, call your mother, drink more water. Ask, gently and honestly, how you're doing with it yourself, not to scold, just to see, and if there's a gap, choose one small way to live it before you say it again. Then let the advice go quiet, and simply breathe.
First yourself. Verse one fifty-eight: set yourself in what is right first, then teach others. Self is the lord of self.
Your line: self is lord of self. First what is proper, then the teaching. A week, done.
